blocks.body:
Walk from the North Pole straight down to the equator, turn left through a right angle, walk a quarter of the way round the equator, turn left through a right angle again, and walk straight back to the pole. You have walked a triangle whose three angles are all right angles: the angle sum is $3\pi/2$, not $\pi$. The excess $\pi/2$ is not an accident. It is exactly the area enclosed (one eighth of the sphere, $\pi R^2/2$) times the Gaussian curvature $1/R^2$.

The Gauss–Bonnet theorem makes this precise for any region on any surface, and then, applied to a whole closed surface, it says that the total curvature is $2\pi$ times the Euler characteristic. This page assumes [[surfaces-curvature]] (first fundamental form, Gaussian curvature, the Theorema Egregium) and the Euler characteristic from [[classification-of-surfaces]].

blocks.title: Geodesic curvature
blocks.body:
Let $S$ be an oriented surface with unit normal $\mathbf{n}$ and let $\alpha(s)$ be a unit-speed curve on $S$. At each point, $T = \alpha'$ and $\mathbf{n} \times T$ are perpendicular unit vectors in the tangent plane, and together with $\mathbf{n}$ they form an orthonormal frame. Since $\alpha''$ is perpendicular to $T$ (see [[curves]]), it splits as
$$\alpha'' = k_n\, \mathbf{n} + \kappa_g\, (\mathbf{n} \times T).$$
The normal part $k_n$ is the normal curvature from [[surfaces-curvature]]; it is forced on the curve by the bending of the surface. The tangential part
$$\kappa_g = \alpha'' \cdot (\mathbf{n} \times T)$$
is the geodesic curvature: how much the curve turns within the surface, measured with a sign (positive when it turns towards $\mathbf{n} \times T$, i.e. to the left as seen from the side the normal points to). The curvature of $\alpha$ as a space curve satisfies $\kappa^2 = k_n^2 + \kappa_g^2$.

An ant on the surface feels only $\kappa_g$, its own steering; indeed $\kappa_g$ depends only on the first fundamental form, as the formula below shows.

blocks.title: Geodesic
blocks.body:
A geodesic on $S$ is a unit-speed curve with $\kappa_g = 0$ everywhere, that is, a curve whose acceleration $\alpha''$ is everywhere perpendicular to the surface.

In words: a geodesic is a curve that never steers left or right within the surface; the only acceleration it has is what is needed to stay on the surface.

blocks.title: Examples of geodesics, and why they matter
blocks.body:
On a plane, geodesics are straight lines. On the sphere $|x| = R$, a great circle traced at unit speed has $\alpha'' = -\alpha / R^2$, which is parallel to the normal, so great circles are geodesics. A circle of latitude other than the equator is not. On a cylinder, unrolling it flat (which preserves the first fundamental form) turns geodesics into straight lines, so the geodesics of the cylinder are the rulings, the circles around it and the helices.

Two standard facts, stated without proof. Through every point, in every tangent direction, there is exactly one geodesic, at least for a short time (it solves a second-order system of differential equations). And a shortest curve on $S$ between two points, if it exists and is smooth, is a geodesic; conversely, short enough pieces of geodesics are shortest. Long geodesics need not be shortest: going the long way round a great circle is a geodesic but not the shortest route.

In coordinates with $F = 0$, write $e_1 = \mathbf{x}_u / \sqrt{E}$, $e_2 = \mathbf{x}_v / \sqrt{G}$, and let $\varphi(s)$ be the angle from $e_1$ to the tangent $\alpha'(s)$. Liouville's formula (stated without proof) expresses the geodesic curvature intrinsically:
$$\kappa_g = \frac{d\varphi}{ds} + \frac{1}{2\sqrt{EG}}\left( G_u \frac{dv}{ds} - E_v \frac{du}{ds} \right).$$
The first term is the turning of the curve relative to the coordinate frame; the second is the turning of the coordinate frame itself.

blocks.title: Local Gauss–Bonnet theorem
blocks.body:
Let $\mathbf{x} : U \to S$ be a patch with $F = 0$, and let $R \subset \mathbf{x}(U)$ be a region homeomorphic to a closed disc whose boundary is a simple closed curve made of smooth arcs, traversed so that $R$ lies to the left (in the sense of $\mathbf{n} \times T$ pointing into $R$). At the corners let $\theta_1, \dots, \theta_m \in (-\pi, \pi)$ be the signed exterior angles, the angles through which the tangent turns. Then
$$\int_{\partial R} \kappa_g \, ds + \iint_R K \, dA + \sum_{i=1}^{m} \theta_i = 2\pi.$$

blocks.title: Proof sketch
blocks.body:
Integrate Liouville's formula round the boundary:
$$\int_{\partial R}\kappa_g\,ds = \int_{\partial R} d\varphi + \oint_{\partial R} P\,du + Q\,dv, \qquad P = -\frac{E_v}{2\sqrt{EG}}, \quad Q = \frac{G_u}{2\sqrt{EG}}.$$
By Green's theorem (see [[vector-calculus]]) in the parameter domain,
$$\oint P\,du + Q\,dv = \iint \left(Q_u - P_v\right) du\,dv = \iint \frac12\left[\Big(\frac{G_u}{\sqrt{EG}}\Big)_u + \Big(\frac{E_v}{\sqrt{EG}}\Big)_v\right] du\,dv = -\iint_R K\,dA,$$
where the last step is the Theorema Egregium formula $K = -\frac{1}{2\sqrt{EG}}[\cdots]$ from [[surfaces-curvature]] together with $dA = \sqrt{EG}\,du\,dv$.

It remains to evaluate the total change of $\varphi$ along the smooth arcs. Going once round a simple closed curve, the tangent direction makes one full turn: the smooth turning plus the jumps $\theta_i$ at the corners add to $2\pi$. This is Hopf's rotation theorem (mentioned in [[curves]]) applied in the parameter plane, after checking that measuring angles with $E, G$ instead of the Euclidean metric does not change the total (deform the metric continuously to the Euclidean one; the total is a multiple of $2\pi$ that varies continuously, hence constant). So $\int d\varphi = 2\pi - \sum \theta_i$, and combining the two displays gives the theorem.

blocks.title: Triangles and caps on the sphere
blocks.body: (a) Show that for a triangle on any surface whose sides are geodesic arcs, with interior angles $\iota_1, \iota_2, \iota_3$, one has $\iota_1 + \iota_2 + \iota_3 = \pi + \iint_\Delta K\, dA$, and check the triangle of the introduction. (b) On the unit sphere, let $R$ be the cap $\theta \le \theta_0$ around the north pole, $0 < \theta_0 < \pi$. Compute the geodesic curvature of its boundary circle and verify the local theorem directly.
blocks.solution:
(a) The sides are geodesics, so $\kappa_g = 0$ on them. Interior and exterior angles are related by $\iota_i = \pi - \theta_i$. The theorem gives $\iint K\, dA + 3\pi - (\iota_1 + \iota_2 + \iota_3) = 2\pi$, which is the formula. For the sphere of radius $R$, $K = 1/R^2$ and the triangle of the introduction covers one eighth of the sphere, area $\pi R^2/2$, so the angle sum is $\pi + \pi/2 = 3\pi/2$: three right angles, as observed. For any geodesic triangle on that sphere, angle excess equals area$/R^2$ (Girard's theorem); on a surface with $K < 0$, angle sums are less than $\pi$.

(b) The boundary is the circle of latitude $\theta = \theta_0$, which has radius $\sin\theta_0$, so its curvature in space is $1/\sin\theta_0$. Its normal curvature is the normal curvature of the unit sphere, $\pm 1$. Hence $\kappa_g^2 = 1/\sin^2\theta_0 - 1 = \cot^2\theta_0$. Taking the outward normal and running the circle anticlockwise as seen from above, so that the cap is on the left, a direct computation gives $\kappa_g = \cot\theta_0$ (positive for $\theta_0 < \pi/2$: the circle turns towards the cap). Liouville's formula agrees: with $u = \theta$, $v = \varphi$, $E = 1$, $G = \sin^2\theta$, the tangent is along $e_2$ so $\varphi$-turning is $0$, and $\frac{G_\theta}{2\sqrt{EG}}\frac{dv}{ds} = \frac{2\sin\theta_0\cos\theta_0}{2\sin\theta_0}\cdot\frac{1}{\sin\theta_0} = \cot\theta_0$.

Now check the theorem. The boundary has length $2\pi\sin\theta_0$ and no corners, so $\int\kappa_g\, ds = 2\pi\cos\theta_0$. The area of the cap is $\int_0^{2\pi}\!\int_0^{\theta_0}\sin\theta\, d\theta\, d\varphi = 2\pi(1 - \cos\theta_0)$, and $K = 1$. The sum is $2\pi\cos\theta_0 + 2\pi(1 - \cos\theta_0) = 2\pi$. For $\theta_0 = \pi/2$ the boundary is the equator, a geodesic, and the hemisphere alone has total curvature $2\pi$. For $\theta_0 > \pi/2$ the cap is more than a hemisphere and $\kappa_g < 0$: the boundary now turns away from the region.

blocks.title: Global Gauss–Bonnet theorem
blocks.body:
Let $S$ be a compact orientable surface (in $\mathbb{R}^3$, or more generally with a Riemannian metric) and $\chi(S)$ its Euler characteristic. Then
$$\iint_S K \, dA = 2\pi\chi(S).$$

Take a triangulation of $S$ fine enough that each triangle lies in a coordinate patch with $F = 0$ and is a disc with three smooth sides; such triangulations exist (a standard fact we assume). Orient every triangle so that it lies to the left of its boundary, using the orientation of $S$. Apply the local theorem to each of the $F$ triangles and add:
$$\sum_{\text{triangles}} \int_{\partial\Delta}\kappa_g\, ds + \iint_S K\, dA + \sum_{\text{all corners}} \theta = 2\pi F.$$
Each edge lies on exactly two triangles, which traverse it in opposite directions; reversing direction changes the sign of $\kappa_g$, so the boundary integrals cancel in pairs. Each corner contributes $\theta = \pi - \iota$, and there are $3F$ corners. Around each vertex the interior angles of the triangles meeting there fill out a full turn, so the interior angles add to $2\pi V$. Hence
$$\iint_S K\, dA = 2\pi F - 3\pi F + 2\pi V = 2\pi V - \pi F.$$
Finally $3F = 2E$, because each triangle has three edges and each edge lies on two triangles, so $-\pi F = 2\pi F - 2\pi E$, and the right side is $2\pi(V - E + F) = 2\pi\chi(S)$.

blocks.title: Consequences for closed surfaces
blocks.body: (a) Check the global theorem on the sphere and on the torus. (b) Show that a compact connected orientable surface with $K > 0$ everywhere is homeomorphic to a sphere, and that a torus cannot carry a metric with $K \ge 0$ everywhere unless $K \equiv 0$. (c) Show that on a surface with $K \le 0$, two geodesics starting from a point $p$ cannot meet again at a point $q$ in such a way that the two arcs from $p$ to $q$ bound a region homeomorphic to a disc.
blocks.solution:
(a) Sphere of radius $R$: $K = 1/R^2$ times area $4\pi R^2$ gives $4\pi = 2\pi \cdot 2$. Torus: on [[surfaces-curvature]] we computed $K\, dA = \cos u\, du\, dv$, whose integral is $0 = 2\pi\cdot 0$. Every closed orientable surface of genus $g$ has total curvature $4\pi(1 - g)$, however it is shaped.

(b) If $K > 0$, then $2\pi\chi = \iint K\, dA > 0$, so $\chi > 0$. By the classification, the only closed orientable surface with $\chi > 0$ is the sphere. On a torus, $\iint K\, dA = 0$; if $K \ge 0$ and $K$ is continuous, this forces $K \equiv 0$.

(c) Suppose the two geodesic arcs bound a disc $R$. Its boundary has two smooth pieces with $\kappa_g = 0$ and two corners, at $p$ and $q$, with exterior angles $\theta_p, \theta_q \in (-\pi, \pi)$. (They cannot be $\pm\pi$: that would mean the two geodesics are tangent at the corner, and then by uniqueness of geodesics with given initial direction they would coincide.) The local theorem gives $\theta_p + \theta_q = 2\pi - \iint_R K\, dA \ge 2\pi$, contradicting $\theta_p + \theta_q < 2\pi$. The same argument shows that on such a surface no simple closed geodesic bounds a disc. On the sphere, by contrast, all great circles through $p$ meet again at $-p$.

blocks.title: Beyond surfaces in space
blocks.body:
Nothing in the global theorem refers to the surrounding space: $K$, $\kappa_g$ and $dA$ depend only on the metric, so the statement holds for any compact orientable surface with a Riemannian metric (see [[riemannian-geometry]]). Since the left side is the same for all metrics, it gives a curvature formula for the topological invariant $\chi$; since the right side is topological, it constrains curvature: a metric of constant curvature on a closed orientable surface of genus $g$ must have positive, zero or negative curvature according as $g = 0$, $g = 1$ or $g \ge 2$.

A close relative is the Poincaré–Hopf theorem (stated without proof): for a smooth tangent vector field on a compact surface with isolated zeros, the sum of the indices of the zeros (how many times the field turns around each zero) equals $\chi(S)$. For the sphere, $\chi = 2 \ne 0$, so every tangent vector field has a zero: you cannot comb a hairy ball flat. In higher dimensions, the Chern–Gauss–Bonnet theorem expresses the Euler characteristic of a compact even-dimensional Riemannian manifold as the integral of a polynomial in its curvature, written with [[differential-forms]]; for non-orientable surfaces the global formula still holds when $dA$ is interpreted as a density.

- The local theorem needs the region to be a disc. For an annulus between two latitude circles, the correct count uses $2\pi\chi(\text{annulus}) = 0$ on the right side, with both boundary circles oriented so the region is on their left.
- Signs: the exterior angle is the turning angle, $\pi$ minus the interior angle, and $\kappa_g$ changes sign when the direction of travel or the normal is reversed. Most errors in applying the theorem come from orientation.
- A geodesic is not always a shortest path, and a shortest path between two points need not be unique (any meridian joins the poles of a sphere).
- Geodesic triangles on a surface whose curvature changes sign can have angle sum greater than, equal to or less than $\pi$ depending on where they are; only the integral of $K$ over the triangle decides.

The global theorem joins [[surfaces-curvature]] to [[classification-of-surfaces]]: total curvature determines $\chi$, hence (with orientability) the topological type. Geodesics on general Riemannian manifolds, together with their minimising property and the Jacobi fields that measure how nearby geodesics spread apart, are the subject of [[riemannian-geometry]]; the characterisation of geodesics as critical points of length or energy is a problem in the [[calculus-of-variations]]. The Euler characteristic also equals the alternating sum of Betti numbers in [[homology]], so Gauss–Bonnet is the first example of a theorem equating an integral of curvature with a homological invariant, a pattern that culminates in the Atiyah–Singer index theorem.

1. A geodesic triangle on the unit sphere has angles $\pi/2$, $\pi/3$ and $\pi/3$. What is its area?
2. Show that on the unit sphere a circle of latitude $\theta = \theta_0$ with $0 < \theta_0 < \pi/2$, run anticlockwise as seen from above, has geodesic curvature $-\cot\theta_0$ with respect to the inward normal, and reconcile this with the computation in the example.
3. Use the global theorem to show that the closed surface of genus $2$ in space has a point of negative Gaussian curvature.
4. A geodesic polygon with $n$ sides on a surface with $K \le 0$ bounds a disc. Show that its interior angles add to at most $(n - 2)\pi$.
